abstract: A central goal of evolutionary genetics is to determine how environmental pressures maintain adaptive genetic variation, and evaluate how this variation is encoded in the genome. We leveraged two powerful approaches to identify genomic regions associated with climatic adaptation, test the genetic basis of climatic adaptation, and predict genomic responses to novel climates: genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of climate niche parameters derived from demographic models and genome-environment associations (GEA) of climatic factors with 2,737,409 loci. The GWAS found 319 unique single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with climate niche parameters derived from demographic models using multi-year manipulative field experiments with Boechera stricta. The GEA detected 154 unique SNPs linked to climatic variation, with only one SNP found in both approaches. Local adaptation via adult survival arose primarily through conditional neutrality, as local alleles outperformed foreign alleles at only one end of the climatic gradient, rather than genetic trade-offs. Candidate genes near these loci were implicated in stress responses. Contrary to expectations, increasing temperatures and accelerating snowmelt timings did not augment the absolute fitness of low elevation genotypes. We found non-linear fitness functions for seedling recruitment at multiple SNPs detected via GWAS, with both conditional neutrality and genetic trade-offs evident in different portions of the climatic gradient. Local maladaptation arose exclusively in GEA SNPs. Our analyses revealed that the hot and dry conditions projected under climate change may rapidly exceed the tolerance of this species. However, we identified 47 SNPs at which evolutionary rescue or assisted migration could ameliorate the reduction in fitness under climate change.
